description_hook: In 2019, physicist Ole Peters published a landmark paper in Nature Physics showing why classic expected-value math misleads real decision-makers. By combining Peters's ergodicity insight with J. L. Kelly's 1956 Bell Labs formula, here is how to build wealth and career systems that never hit zero.

scenes.headline: The Coin Flip That Gains 5% and Still Destroys You
scenes.stat_label: GROUP AVERAGE GAIN • INDIVIDUAL TIME DECAY
bullets: Heads raises your wealth +50%; tails cuts your wealth -40%
1,000 strangers flipping once average +5% richer overall
1 person flipping repeatedly loses 10% every head-tail pair
scenes.narration: Suppose someone offers you a fair coin toss on your entire net worth. Every time it lands heads, your wealth jumps fifty percent. Every time it lands tails, your wealth drops forty percent. Standard textbook expected value says you gain five percent per toss, so you should play all afternoon. Yet watch what actually happens to one real person over time. Start with one hundred dollars: win fifty percent to reach one hundred fifty, then lose forty percent on the next toss, and you drop to ninety dollars. One win plus one loss leaves you ten percent poorer.
scenes.source: Ole Peters, 'The ergodicity problem in economics', Nature Physics (2019)

scenes.headline: Ole Peters's 2019 Nature Physics Breakthrough
scenes.left_body: 1,000 parallel players flip once -> few lucky jackpots pull mean up +5%
scenes.right_body: 1 human plays 1,000 sequential steps -> wealth decays ~5.1% per flip
scenes.narration: In 2019, physicist Ole Peters explained this paradox in Nature Physics. For centuries, economic models treated the ensemble average, the mean across a thousand parallel people at one snapshot in time, as identical to the time average, the path experienced by one person living through sequential years. A system where those two averages match is called ergodic. Real wealth, health, and reputation are strictly non-ergodic. In the coin game, a tiny handful of parallel players flip twenty straight heads and become billionaires, skewing the crowd average upward while nearly every individual player steadily bleeds toward zero.
scenes.source: Ole Peters, Nature Physics, Vol. 15, pp. 1216-1221 (2019)

scenes.tag: CHAPTER 3 • THE ABSORBING BARRIER OF RUIN
scenes.headline: Why Anything Multiplied by Zero Stays Zero Forever
scenes.stat_label: THE IRREVERSIBLE CLIFF IN MULTIPLICATIVE GAMES
bullets: Additive games let you bounce back from flat ground
Multiplicative compounding stops permanently at an absorbing barrier
Russian roulette has high 1-round payout and 0% long-run survival
scenes.narration: Non-ergodic traps exist wherever gains and losses multiply rather than add, especially near an absorbing barrier called ruin. Multiply thirty years of brilliant fifteen-percent returns by a single zero, and the final product is zero forever. You cannot average your way back out of bankruptcy, permanent burnout, or a shattered reputation by pointing to what happened to nine other people in a spreadsheet. Think of Russian roulette: five chambers out of six pay a massive prize on a single pull, yet play sequentially across enough Tuesday mornings and survival drops to zero.
scenes.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Skin in the Game (2018); Ole Peters (2019)

scenes.headline: How Position Sizing Turns Decay Into Compounding
scenes.stat_label: 25% STAKES TURN A LOSING GAME POSITIVE
scenes.stat_subtext: Same +50% / -40% coin: 100% stake decays -> 25% stake compounds
scenes.narration: Here is the empowering twist discovered by Bell Labs physicist John Kelly Jr. in 1956. You do not have to walk away from that biased fifty-up, forty-down coin game; you simply have to stop betting your whole pile. If you wager only twenty-five percent of your capital on each toss and keep seventy-five percent in safe reserves, a heads win lifts your total portfolio twelve point five percent, while a tails loss trims just ten percent. Pair one win with one loss now, and one hundred dollars grows to one hundred one dollars and twenty-five cents. Sizing flips decay into compounding.
scenes.source: J. L. Kelly Jr., Bell System Technical Journal (1956); Peters (2019)

scenes.headline: Spotting Hidden Ruin Risks in Everyday Decisions
scenes.left_body: Margin debt, zero cash runway, ethical shortcuts, 80-hour burnout
scenes.right_body: 6-month cash reserve, capped bets, trusted craft, steady pace
scenes.narration: Once you wear the ergodicity lens, hidden traps jump out across everyday finance and career choices. Buying stocks on margin looks clever during calm years, until one sharp recession forces a liquidation at the exact bottom, locking you out of the recovery. Living with zero emergency savings turns a routine layoff into high-interest credit card debt. Cutting an ethical corner to hit one quarterly bonus puts thirty years of career trust on a single spin of the wheel. Conversely, holding a boring six-month cash reserve looks suboptimal on a bull-market chart, yet guarantees you never sell under duress.

scenes.headline: Install the 3-Shield Survival-First Operating System
scenes.stat_label: ELIMINATE RUIN • CAP STAKES • COMPOUND TIME
bullets: 1. Zero-Ruin Filter: never stake rent cash, health, or reputation
2. Fractional Sizing: cap single speculative bets at 5% to 10%
3. Forced-Sale Immunity: hold 6 months of lean living costs liquid
scenes.narration: Apply survival math this week using three concrete shields. Shield one is the Zero-Ruin Filter: refuse any opportunity, no matter how high the advertised average return, if its worst-case outcome impairs your health, your integrity, or your basic solvency. Shield two is Fractional Position Sizing: cap any single speculative stock, angel check, or side venture at five to ten percent of your net worth so even a total wipeout leaves ninety percent of your engine intact. Shield three is Forced-Sale Immunity: maintain six months of lean expenses in liquid treasury cash so your compounding line stays unbroken for decades.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin framework based on Peters (2019) & Kelly (1956) (advice)
